title: Capitalism & Market Economies
description: Property rights, labor markets, varieties of capitalism — Smith to Hall & Soskice

concepts.title: What Capitalism Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Capitalism is best defined not by markets alone — markets predate capitalism by millennia — but by the combination of three features: private ownership of the means of production, wage labour as the dominant form of work, and capital accumulation through reinvestment of profit as the system's central dynamic. Modern capitalism emerged in Western Europe roughly between the 16th and 19th centuries through the enclosure of common land, the rise of joint-stock companies, the spread of factory production, and the industrial revolution.

Several theorists have made this definition precise. Karl Marx's analysis (covered separately in the politics-theory topic) treated capitalism as a class system in which a small bourgeoisie owns the means of production and a much larger proletariat sells its labour for wages, with profit deriving from the gap between wages paid and value produced. Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) emphasised the cultural transformation — the rationalisation of economic life and the emergence of saving and investment as ends in themselves — that distinguished modern capitalism from earlier commercial economies.

What is consistent across these accounts is that capitalism is a historically specific economic system, not a synonym for "markets" or "trade." Markets are old; wage labour at scale, joint-stock companies, central banking, and self-reinforcing capital accumulation are recent. Most political economy concerns the question of how this system reproduces itself, what it produces, and what it leaves out.

concepts.title: The Smith-Marshall Synthesis: How Markets Coordinate
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical case for capitalism, articulated by Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) and refined by neoclassical economists from Alfred Marshall onwards, is that competitive markets coordinate dispersed activity through the price system. Smith's "invisible hand" is the metaphor: individuals pursuing their own interests through voluntary exchange produce, as if by design, an outcome that no single actor planned and that often serves the broader public.

The technical foundation is the First Welfare Theorem: under competition, complete markets, and absence of externalities, market equilibria are Pareto-efficient — no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. The result is mathematically elegant; the conditions are demanding. Real markets are rarely competitive (firms have market power), rarely complete (insurance and information markets fail), and rarely free of externalities (pollution, financial-system spillovers). Welfare economics' second theorem allows for redistribution before markets operate, restoring the efficiency case in principle.

The Austrian tradition (Hayek, Mises) made a different but related case: markets are not just efficient at static allocation but uniquely good at using dispersed knowledge. No central planner can possibly know the local information — what a particular farmer's soil supports, what a particular consumer values — that prices encode and transmit. This Hayekian argument is the strongest one against detailed central planning and remains the basis of much classical-liberal political economy. It does not, however, decide the harder question of how much market and how much state in any actually-existing economy.

concepts.title: Varieties of Capitalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Existing capitalist economies differ in important ways. Peter Hall and David Soskice's Varieties of Capitalism (2001) framework distinguishes two main types of advanced capitalism.

Liberal Market Economies (LMEs) — the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand — coordinate primarily through markets and arm's-length contracts. Labour markets are flexible; corporate finance comes through stock markets; firms compete on the basis of innovation, especially radical innovation; vocational training is generic; welfare states are smaller and means-tested.

Coordinated Market Economies (CMEs) — Germany, the Nordics, Switzerland, Austria, the Netherlands, Japan in modified form — coordinate through long-term relationships and institutions. Labour markets are more regulated, with stronger unions and works councils; firms get capital from long-term bank relationships; competition emphasises incremental innovation in established industries; vocational training is industry-specific and apprenticeship-based; welfare states are universalist and generous.

The Hall-Soskice framework is contested in detail and has been extended (Bruno Amable's Five Capitalisms, 2003, adds Mediterranean, Asian, and emerging-market variants), but the core insight has held up well. There is no single "capitalism"; the economies of the OECD are recognisably different systems with different strengths, weaknesses, and political coalitions sustaining them. The question of which variant is preferable, or whether the differences are converging or diverging, is one of the central ongoing arguments in comparative political economy.

title: State Capitalism & Mixed Economies
description: Developmental states, SOEs, industrial policy — when the state directs the market

concepts.title: The Mixed Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
Almost no large modern economy is purely capitalist or purely socialist. The standard term for the combination is mixed economy: predominantly private ownership and markets, with significant state ownership, regulation, and direct provision in particular sectors. The midcentury social-democratic settlement — public-service broadcasters, nationalised utilities, universal healthcare and pensions, progressive taxation, strong labour protections — was the form mixed economies took across most of postwar Western Europe.

The boundary between "capitalist" and "socialist" or "state" economies is therefore not sharp. France's post-1945 dirigisme involved active industrial planning by the state through plans, indicative targets, and large public-sector firms (Renault, EDF, SNCF). Sweden's mid-20th-century model had high taxes and a large public sector but mostly privately owned firms. The UK after 1945 nationalised coal, rail, steel, and utilities; Margaret Thatcher's privatisations after 1979 reversed most of those. Each shift was contested and reversible.

The 21st-century debate is less about whether to have a mixed economy than about which mix. Industrial policy — the state actively supporting particular sectors — has been making a comeback even in formerly free-market jurisdictions. The US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) and CHIPS Act (2022), the EU's Green Industrial Plan, and the UK's industrial strategy all signal a return to active state shaping of the economy after several decades of relative laissez-faire.

concepts.title: Developmental States in East Asia
concepts.contentHtml:
The most studied non-Anglo-American capitalist successes are the East Asian developmental states. Chalmers Johnson's MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982) coined the term and the framework. A developmental state pursues industrialisation as an explicit national project: the state identifies strategic sectors, channels capital toward them through state banks or directed credit, protects them from foreign competition during a developmental window, then exposes them to international markets once they reach competitive scale.

The classic cases are Japan (Ministry of International Trade and Industry, MITI), South Korea (the Park Chung-hee era's chaebol-state alliances), and Taiwan (Industrial Technology Research Institute and the technology cluster around TSMC and the Hsinchu Science Park). Each combined private-sector dynamism with active state guidance — closer to a coordinated market economy than to either pure capitalism or socialism.

The model has been controversial. Liberal economists (Anne Krueger, others) have argued that the East Asian success was actually due to market-friendly policies despite the state interventions. Heterodox economists (Alice Amsden, Ha-Joon Chang, Robert Wade) have argued the interventions were essential. The cases of countries that tried to copy the model and failed — many Southeast Asian, African, and Latin American attempts — suggest that effective state capacity, not just intervention, is necessary. Whatever the verdict, the developmental-state experience reshaped what is taken to be possible in capitalist political economy.

concepts.title: China: State Capitalism at Scale
concepts.contentHtml:
The largest contemporary case of state-led capitalism is China. The 1978 reforms launched what the CCP calls "socialism with Chinese characteristics" — markets and private firms allowed to operate within a system where the Communist Party retains political control and substantial economic coordination. The result has been the largest sustained growth episode in modern history: over 40 years of average GDP growth above 9%, the largest poverty reduction in human history, and the emergence of the world's second-largest economy.

The institutional arrangement is hybrid. Roughly one-third of the Chinese economy operates as state-owned enterprises (SOEs), often dominant in strategic sectors (energy, banking, telecommunications, transport, defence). The other two-thirds is private but operates under explicit Party guidance through Party committees in firms, control of capital allocation through state banks, and increasingly direct CCP intervention in the largest private companies (the 2020 cancellation of Ant Group's IPO is the textbook case). Industrial policy — "Made in China 2025", the dual-circulation strategy, the Belt and Road Initiative — channels resources toward sectors the Party identifies as strategically important.

Whether the system is best called "state capitalism", "party-state capitalism" (Pearson, Rithmire, Tsai's framing), or something else is a matter of definition. What is empirically clear is that the largest economy outside the Western capitalist tradition has spent four decades demonstrating that there are durable alternatives to the LME and CME models — alternatives that are themselves sustained variants of capitalism, but operating under very different political constraints.

title: Trade & Globalization
description: Comparative advantage, GATT/WTO, supply chains, deglobalization

concepts.title: Comparative Advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical case for international trade is David Ricardo's 1817 doctrine of comparative advantage. Even when one country can produce everything more efficiently than another (absolute advantage), both countries can still benefit from trade if they specialise in goods where their relative productivity advantage is greatest. The mathematics of the standard two-good two-country example, taught in every introductory economics course, shows that voluntary trade can leave both parties better off in real terms.

The result generalises. Modern trade theory — Heckscher-Ohlin, the Stolper-Samuelson theorem, the work of Paul Krugman on intra-industry trade — has refined the conditions under which trade produces gains and the conditions under which it produces winners and losers within countries. The general claim that trade increases aggregate national income is well supported empirically; the question of how those gains are distributed and how losers are compensated is much more contested.

That distributional question matters because trade in modern manufacturing-intensive economies has produced significant localised losses. The China shock literature (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, 2013 onwards) found that US manufacturing communities exposed to Chinese import competition after WTO accession suffered persistent declines in employment, wages, and population — losses that were not adequately compensated by the aggregate gains. The political consequences of those concentrated losses — declining trust in institutions, support for populist movements, and demands for industrial policy — have reshaped trade politics across many democracies in the 21st century.

concepts.title: GATT, the WTO, and the Postwar Trade Order
concepts.contentHtml:
The institutional architecture of postwar trade was the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, 1947), evolved through eight multilateral negotiation rounds into the World Trade Organization (WTO, 1995). The system reduced average tariffs across member countries from around 22% in 1947 to under 5% by the early 2000s, and progressively expanded to cover services (GATS), intellectual property (TRIPS), and a binding dispute-settlement mechanism with an Appellate Body.

The expansion of the system was paired with the rise of global value chains: production processes that span multiple countries, with components crossing borders multiple times before final assembly. The iPhone, designed in California, with chips from Taiwan and South Korea, displays from Japan, batteries from China, assembly in China and India, is the textbook case. Such chains drove enormous productivity gains and were the operational mechanism through which globalisation transformed the world economy from the 1990s onwards.

The system has been straining since the 2008 financial crisis. The Doha round of WTO negotiations (launched 2001) has effectively failed; the WTO Appellate Body has been incapacitated since 2019 by US blocking of judicial appointments; bilateral and regional trade deals (CPTPP, RCEP, USMCA, the EU's deals) have proliferated as substitutes for stalled multilateralism. The post-1945 commitment to a single, rules-based, near-universal trade system is, on most readings, in retreat.

concepts.title: Deglobalisation, Friend-shoring, and the Future of Trade
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2010s and 2020s have produced sustained discussion of deglobalisation — a partial reversal of the cross-border integration of the previous decades. The drivers are multiple: the costs of supply-chain concentration revealed by the Covid-19 pandemic; the strategic concerns about Chinese dominance in critical sectors; the political backlash against trade-related job losses in advanced economies; the post-2022 sanctions architecture against Russia.

The data on actual deglobalisation is more nuanced. Global trade as a share of world GDP has plateaued around 60% since 2008 rather than continuing its earlier sharp rise — significant as a structural break, but well short of a full retreat. Foreign direct investment flows have shifted away from China toward other emerging markets (Vietnam, India, Mexico) and toward reshoring within advanced economies. Supply-chain restructuring in strategic sectors — semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, critical minerals — is real and ongoing.

The evolving vocabulary captures the shift. Reshoring brings production back to the home country. Nearshoring moves it to geographically nearby countries. Friend-shoring (a term US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen used in 2022) moves it to politically aligned countries. De-risking diversifies exposure to single-jurisdiction risk without full decoupling. Whether these adjustments produce a fundamentally different trade order or a modified continuation of the old one will be visible only in retrospect; the central commercial question of the 2020s is which sectors restructure and which do not.

title: Development & Underdevelopment
description: Modernization, dependency, institutions — why some nations stay poor

concepts.title: Modernization Theory and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
The first systematic post-war framework for thinking about why some countries developed and others did not was modernization theory. Walt Rostow's The Stages of Economic Growth: A Non-Communist Manifesto (1960) argued that all societies pass through five stages — traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, age of high mass consumption — and that development was a matter of accelerating that universal trajectory through investment, education, and (often) Western capital and advice.

The theory was politically convenient for Cold War US foreign policy: development could be achieved within capitalism, modelled on the West, and aided by external assistance. The empirical record was mixed. Some countries — Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore — achieved sustained transitions broadly compatible with the framework. Many others — large parts of Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, South Asia — did not, despite decades of aid and policy advice.

The first major challenge was dependency theory, developed in 1960s and 1970s Latin America by Raúl Prebisch, André Gunder Frank, Fernando Cardoso, and others. Their claim was that the world economy was structured into core and periphery: peripheral economies were not behind on a universal development path but actively underdeveloped by their position in the global system, exporting cheap commodities and importing expensive manufactures, with surplus extracted by core capital. Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems theory (from 1974) generalised the framework historically.

concepts.title: The Institutional Turn
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant contemporary framework is institutional. Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James Robinson's widely-cited 2001 paper "The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development" argued that the institutional choices made by colonial powers — extractive vs inclusive — set countries on durable paths from which they have struggled to deviate. Inclusive institutions protect property rights, enforce contracts, and constrain elites; they support broad-based investment and innovation. Extractive institutions concentrate power and economic gain in narrow elites; they may produce growth (the Soviet Union, China through 1976, Saudi oil monarchy) but rarely the kind of innovation-driven, broad-based prosperity inclusive institutions sustain.

Acemoglu and Robinson's Why Nations Fail (2012) made the popular argument: prosperity follows institutions, not geography or culture, and political institutions are the deepest determinant. The framework is contested in detail — Jared Diamond's geographical determinism, Gregory Clark's cultural arguments, the broader 'unified growth theory' tradition all push back — but the institutional case has been broadly persuasive in development economics over the past two decades. Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson received the 2024 Nobel Prize for the body of work it summarises.

The policy implications are uncomfortable. Externally-driven institutional reform is hard; what works in one country often fails in another; the 2000s "good governance" agenda's record is mixed; and the deep political constraints that produce extractive institutions in the first place rarely loosen on outside instruction. Development, on this account, is fundamentally a domestic political process — one that external actors can support at the margins but cannot substitute for.

concepts.title: What Has Worked: The Asian Miracle and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Despite the difficulty of the development problem, the past 70 years have produced extraordinary successes. The four Asian Tigers — South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore — went from per-capita incomes comparable to Sub-Saharan Africa in the 1950s to advanced-economy status by the 2000s. China's reform era has lifted around 800 million people out of extreme poverty, the largest sustained reduction in human history. Vietnam has followed a similar though smaller trajectory. India's post-1991 reforms produced sustained if uneven growth.

The shared features of these successes — analysed by the World Bank's 1993 East Asian Miracle report and refined since — include high rates of saving and investment, broad-based education investment, gradual integration into world trade, active industrial policy in early stages, and (crucially) effective state capacity. The list is suggestive rather than a recipe: many countries have tried elements without producing sustained transitions.

The harder cases — most of Sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America, fragile Middle Eastern states — illustrate the constraints. Where state capacity is low, institutions extractive, security weak, and external shocks frequent (commodity-price crashes, conflict, climate stress), even good policy intentions often fail to produce sustained transitions. The post-2000 increase in extreme-poverty reduction has been concentrated heavily in Asia; African progress, while real, has been uneven and partially reversed by recent shocks. Development remains, as it has been for decades, the central unsolved problem of global political economy.

title: Monetary & Fiscal Power
description: Central banks, reserve currencies, sanctions, financial statecraft

concepts.title: Central Banks and Monetary Power
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern central banks are the most powerful single economic-policy institutions in most countries, operating with various forms of independence from elected governments. The Federal Reserve (1913), the European Central Bank (1998), the Bank of England (operationally independent since 1997), the Bank of Japan, the People's Bank of China, and their counterparts set short-term interest rates, manage money supply, and (since 2008–9) operate on the size and composition of their balance sheets through quantitative-easing and quantitative-tightening operations.

The independence doctrine emerged from the lessons of 1970s stagflation: politicians have systematic incentives to choose looser monetary policy than is good for long-run inflation, and binding the central bank's hands produces better outcomes. The empirical evidence supports the case for independence in advanced economies; it is less clear in emerging economies where central banks face very different constraints. The recent inflation episodes of 2021–2024 have produced the biggest test of central-bank independence in decades, with politicians on both left and right pressuring central banks across many countries.

Modern central banking has expanded well beyond inflation. The 2008 financial crisis and 2020 Covid response saw central banks become massive lenders, asset purchasers, and de-facto fiscal actors. The quantitative easing programmes alone created multiple trillions of dollars in central-bank balance-sheet expansion. Whether the political legitimacy of unelected central banks can sustain this expanded role over the long run is one of the central questions of contemporary monetary economics.

concepts.title: The Dollar System and Reserve Currencies
concepts.contentHtml:
The international monetary system is currently organised around the US dollar as the primary reserve and trading currency. Roughly 59% of global central-bank foreign-exchange reserves are held in dollars (down from a peak of around 70% in the early 2000s); the dollar is on one side of nearly 90% of foreign-exchange transactions; oil and most other major commodities are traded primarily in dollars; the SWIFT messaging system that underpins international payments is concentrated in dollar-denominated activity.

The arrangement is the product of historical accident and accumulated infrastructure rather than any single design. The 1944 Bretton Woods system pegged other currencies to the dollar, which was in turn pegged to gold. After Nixon's 1971 closure of the gold window, the system became a free-floating dollar standard. The dollar's role has been sustained by US economic size, deep and liquid financial markets, the rule of law, and the absence of credible alternatives at scale.

The combination produces what former French finance minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing called America's "exorbitant privilege": the US can run persistent current-account deficits financed by foreign demand for its assets, can borrow cheaply in its own currency, and can use the dollar's centrality as a tool of foreign policy. Challenges to dollar dominance — the euro since 1999, the renminbi more recently — have made marginal inroads but have not produced a credible alternative. Whether the dollar's role survives the next decade depends on US policy as much as on rivals' efforts.

concepts.title: Financial Statecraft: Sanctions and Weaponised Interdependence
concepts.contentHtml:
The dollar's centrality has, especially since 2001, been weaponised through financial sanctions. The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) maintains the Specially Designated Nationals list, restricting US-person transactions with named individuals, firms, and governments. Secondary sanctions threaten non-US entities with loss of dollar-clearing access if they transact with sanctioned parties — effectively coercing global compliance with US lists.

The post-2014 Russia sanctions, expanded dramatically in 2022, illustrate the scale of contemporary financial statecraft. The freezing of around $300 billion in Russian central-bank reserves held in Western jurisdictions; the cutting of major Russian banks from SWIFT; the price cap on Russian oil exports; the parallel sanctions regimes on Iran, Venezuela, North Korea, and others — all draw their force from the dollar's centrality and the secondary-sanctions threat.

Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman's Underground Empire (2023) and earlier work introduced the concept of weaponised interdependence — the way the very networks of trade, finance, and information that produce the gains from globalisation also create chokepoints that powerful states can exploit. Sanctions are one such chokepoint; export controls on advanced semiconductors are another; the SWIFT messaging system is a third. The strategic implication is that the most networked economy in the system also has the most coercive levers — and that targets of those levers (Russia, China, Iran) are now investing heavily in alternative payment systems, gold reserves, and bilateral trade in non-dollar currencies. Whether they can build credible alternatives at scale is the central question of the next phase of international monetary politics.

title: Inequality & Redistribution
description: Welfare states, taxation, Piketty — the politics of who gets what

concepts.title: Measuring Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
Economic inequality is measured along several distinct dimensions, and conflating them produces much of the public confusion about whether inequality is rising. Income inequality measures the distribution of annual earnings; wealth inequality measures the distribution of accumulated assets and is typically far more concentrated than income; consumption inequality measures actual material standards of living and tends to be the least concentrated of the three.

The standard summary measure is the Gini coefficient, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything). Among advanced economies, post-tax-and-transfer Gini coefficients run from around 0.25 in the Nordics to 0.39 in the United States. Top-share measures — what fraction of income or wealth accrues to the top 1% or top 0.1% — capture concentration at the very top better than the Gini does, and were the focus of Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman's influential reconstructions of long-run inequality data.

The empirical picture from this work is well-established. Income concentration in the US, UK, and (more weakly) most other advanced economies fell between roughly 1930 and 1980 and rose sharply afterwards, with the top 1% income share in the US roughly doubling from around 10% to over 20% between 1980 and 2020. Wealth concentration has followed a similar but lagged path. Continental Europe and Japan have seen smaller increases. The global picture is different: between-country inequality has been falling thanks to Chinese and Indian growth, even as within-country inequality has risen in most major economies.

concepts.title: Welfare States and Redistribution
concepts.contentHtml:
The modern welfare state — the dense network of taxes, transfers, and public services that redistributes income and pools risk — is the most important single redistributive institution in advanced economies. Bismarck's late-19th-century social-insurance schemes (sickness, accident, old-age) provided the template; the post-1945 expansion under Beveridge in Britain, the New Deal and Great Society in the US, and Social Democratic programmes across Continental Europe built it out to its modern scale.

The Danish sociologist Gøsta Esping-Andersen's Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990) classified welfare states into three regime types. Liberal welfare states (US, UK, Canada, Australia) provide modest, often means-tested benefits; reliance on private provision is high; redistribution is limited. Conservative-corporatist welfare states (Germany, France, Italy, Austria) link benefits to employment-based contributions; protection is generous for those in stable work; redistribution across class lines is moderate. Social-democratic welfare states (Nordic countries) provide universalist benefits funded by broad-based taxation; redistribution is high; female labour-force participation is supported by extensive public childcare. The typology has been extended and contested but remains the standard framework.

The fiscal redistribution performed by these systems is large. In most advanced economies, taxes-and-transfers reduce the Gini coefficient by between 10 and 20 points relative to market-income inequality. The US system, surprisingly, performs less redistribution than European peers despite having the highest pre-tax inequality — a mismatch some economists call the American paradox. The political-economy explanation involves race, federal structure, and the historical weakness of the American left, all of which have shaped what kind of welfare state was politically buildable.

concepts.title: Piketty and the Politics of Wealth
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013, English 2014) was the most influential economics book of the 2010s. Its central empirical claim is that, over the long run, the rate of return on capital (r) tends to exceed the growth rate of the economy (g) — "r > g" — and that this gap drives a tendency toward rising wealth concentration absent strong countervailing forces (wars, depressions, progressive taxation, broad-based growth).

The argument is contested in detail. Critics including Matthew Rognlie have argued that the rising capital share Piketty documents is concentrated heavily in housing, raising different policy questions than Piketty's preferred wealth tax. Others have questioned whether the historical data Piketty assembled support his theoretical model. But the broad empirical pattern — large 20th-century compression of inequality, post-1980 reversal — is now widely accepted, and Piketty and his collaborators' construction of long-run wealth and income series is one of the major empirical achievements in economics of the past two decades.

The policy debate sparked by Piketty has produced concrete proposals: a global wealth tax (Piketty), reformed income taxation that closes the capital-gains preference, expanded estate taxation, and stronger labour-side institutions. Politically, almost none of these have been implemented. The 2020s saw revived discussion of wealth taxes (Warren in the US, several European countries), but the constitutional and administrative challenges of taxing wealth — capital flight, valuation difficulties, the political organisation of the very rich — have so far prevented major adoption. The politics of who gets what remains the oldest question in political economy and the one on which clean answers are rarest.
